member.name: M:SIPSorceryMedia.Abstractions.RawImage.GetBuffer
member.summary: Copies the pixel data into a new managed array.
member.returns: The copied pixel data, or null if this image has no usable dimensions.

remarks.para: This is the safe way to consume a decoded frame. points at memory owned by the decoder and is only valid for the duration of the callback, so a handler that does anything after it returns, such as marshalling to a UI thread, must take a copy first. The returned array has no such restriction and can be held for as long as needed.

The copy costs a fraction of a millisecond even at high resolutions, but allocates a new array per frame. Use with a re-used buffer to avoid that, or directly when the frame is fully consumed before the handler returns.

member.summary: Copies the pixel data into a buffer supplied by the caller, so a buffer can be re-used across frames rather than allocating one per frame as does.

member.summary: Copies the pixel data straight into unmanaged memory, such as the Scan0 of a locked bitmap, with no intermediate managed array.
member.param: The destination buffer, which must hold at least bytes.

member.name: M:SIPSorceryMedia.Abstractions.RawImage.CopyTo(System.IntPtr,System.Int32)
member.summary: Copies the pixel data straight into unmanaged memory whose rows are a different length to this image's, such as a GDI+ bitmap that pads each row to a multiple of four bytes.
member.param: The destination buffer.
The byte offset between the start of one destination row and the next.
member.returns: The number of bytes copied.

remarks.para: This is the zero allocation path: one copy, decoder buffer straight to destination. It is only usable while is valid, meaning inside the callback that supplied this image, so the destination has to be ready at that point.

Take care when the destination belongs to a UI toolkit. Writing to a bitmap from the decoder's thread while the UI thread paints that same bitmap is a data race, and GDI+ in particular throws rather than tearing. Either render synchronously, or copy into memory the UI owns exclusively, or use / and defer.

member.exception: Thrown when is a null pointer.
Thrown when is not greater than zero.

example.para: The example ShowFrame method below copies a decoded 24 bits per pixel frame into a bitmap the calling application owns and displays it.
The copy runs on the decoder's callback thread, the only place is guaranteed to be valid.
That thread also carries the media transport, so it needs to do the minimum amount of work possible. Anything slow on it holds up the packets still arriving.

The mechanism used is to rotate two bitmaps so the one being written is never the one the picture box is painting, which GDI+ would throw on: the UI thread hands the previous bitmap back once it has been replaced and it will be used for the next frame copy.

The bitmaps are allocated once and re-used until the frame size changes. Allocating one per frame costs several times more than the copy itself and, at 1080p and above, produces enough garbage to stall the application.
Note GDI+'s Format24bppRgb is B,G,R in memory despite the name, which is why a Bgr sample can be copied into it verbatim.
_spareBmp, _form, _picBox and logger are fields of the calling form.

member.name: T:SIPSorceryMedia.Abstractions.IVideoSink
member.summary: Interface to represent a video sink.

remarks.para: Decoded frames are handed to subscribers as borrowed memory that is only valid for the duration of the event handler. Decoders re-use a single conversion buffer for every frame, so the pointer supplied with one frame is overwritten by the next, and the managed array supplied to the byte[] overload becomes unreachable as soon as the handler returns.

A handler that renders the frame synchronously can use the sample in place. A handler that defers the work, for example marshalling to a UI thread, must copy the sample first. Wrapping the buffer in something that outlives the call, such as a Bitmap constructed over the pointer, reads memory that has since been overwritten or freed.

The recommended pattern is to copy each frame into a bitmap the caller owns, allocated once and re-used until the frame dimensions change. Allocating a bitmap per frame costs several times more than the copy itself and, at high resolutions, generates enough garbage to stall the application.
